doc.title: Benny Powell interviewed by Monk Rowe, New York City, New York, July 27, 1995 [interview 1 of 2]

title: Fate, preparation, business sense and understanding people
summary: Powell says being good is not enough; successful musicians know business and understand people.

story.theme_name: Teaching jazz: schools, students and advice to the young
story.community_name: Advice to young musicians starting out

blocks.x: You know it’s funny sometimes how fate lends you that break you need.

Oh, always does. Hindsight. Well I guess this is a bit away from our thought, but in Duke Ellington’s book, I love the opening of the book because I can’t remember, I can’t quote it verbatim, but he said when he first went out his house down the driveway and got to the fence when it was time to go out, there was always someone there to tell him which way to go if he wanted to go somewhere. And that’s happened throughout his career. He said whenever he needed something — but I guess it’s our own awareness that does it, anyway. You know if you are aware, something tells you and you are aware of it. If not, they tell you but you’re not aware of it so it doesn’t do you much good.
Some people say that if you really prepare and you’re really good at what you do your chance will come.

I think a bit of that with a bit of plain common sense too, realizing, well I know a lot of musicians believe that. So they think it’s not really necessary for them to know business, know how to read contracts, know how to go and get a job, because if it’s good it will come. But I say perhaps it will help you to stay in a position after you get there. But just being good, I’ve seen too many real good people not go anywhere because they didn’t have the whole picture together. Most of the guys who are successful are pretty good businessmen, pretty good talkers and they have other talents other than their playing, what they play.
In other words they understand the industry. They understand marketing.

Yes. Most of all they understand humankind. They understand people. So whoever you’re talking to, whether you be president or a porter, they’re still made of the same thing. He’s got two eyes, two ears, and stuff you know. And I think that’s sort of the commonality jazz musicians make among people. Because we meet so many people, and so I think we’re a little more experienced than the average person too. So when we meet somebody, we’re involved right away. We see a lot about that person.
